questions.subject: network-theory
questions.question: A square waveform as shown in figure is applied across \(1\text{ mH}\) ideal inductor. The current through inductor is a
options: triangular wave with peak amplitude of \(0.5\text{ Amp}\).
triangular wave with peak amplitude of \(1.0\text{ Amp}\).
triangular wave with peak amplitude of \(2.0\text{ Amp}\).
sine wave with peak amplitude of \(0.5\text{ Amp}\).
questions.explanation: For an inductor, \[i_L(t) = \frac{1}{L}\int v_L(t)\,dt\] Thus, the current through an inductor is the integration of the applied voltage. A square wave, when integrated, produces a triangular waveform. Given, \(L=1~\text{mH}\) The applied voltage is +1~V for \(0.5~\text{ms}\), followed by -1~V for the next \(0.5~\text{ms}\). The change in current during the positive half-cycle is \[\Delta i = \frac{V}{L}\Delta t = \frac{1}{1\times10^{-3}} \left(0.5\times10^{-3}\right) = 0.5~\text{A}\] Similarly, during the negative half-cycle, \(\Delta i = -0.5~\text{A}\) Hence, the current increases linearly to \(0.5~\text{A}\) and then decreases linearly back to zero, repeating periodically. Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{A. }\text{Triangular wave with peak amplitude of }0.5~\text{A}}\]

questions.subject: network-theory
questions.question: The value of current through the 1F capacitor of figure is
questions.explanation: The problem involves calculating the current through a specific branch (the \(1\,\text{F}\) capacitor). We first convert the network components to reactances,then performing a Delta-to-Star (\(\Delta\text{-Y}\)) transformation, and analyzing the simplified bridge network. Step 1: Conversion of Circuit Elements to Reactances The source frequency from the voltage expression \(2\sin(100t)\) is: \[\omega = 100\,\text{rad/s}\] The impedances of the elements are calculated as follows: For the \(1\,\text{F}\) capacitor: \[Z_{C1} = \frac{-j}{\omega C} = \frac{-j}{100 \times 1} = -0.01j\,\Omega\] For the \(0.5\,\text{F}\) capacitor: \[Z_{C2} = \frac{-j}{\omega C} = \frac{-j}{0.5 \times 100} = -0.02j\,\Omega\] For the \(1\,\text{H}\) inductor: \[Z_{L} = j\omega L = j(100 \times 1) = j100\,\Omega\] Step 2: Delta to Star (\(\Delta\text{-Y}\)) Transformation By converting the outer delta network comprising the reactances into an equivalent star network, the calculated star impedances are: For \(Z_1\): \[Z_1 = \frac{(1 - 0.02j)(1 - 0.02j)}{1 - 0.02j + 1 - 0.02j + 2 + j100} = \frac{0.9996 - 0.04j}{4 + j99.96} \approx 0\,\Omega\] For \(Z_2\) and \(Z_3\): \[Z_2 = Z_3 = \frac{(1 - 0.02j)(2 + j100)}{4 + j99.96} = \frac{4 + j99.96}{4 + j99.96} = 1\,\Omega\] Step 3: Analysis of the Simplified Circuit Replacing the delta section with its star equivalent transforms the circuit configuration into a balanced Wheatstone bridge network consisting of four \(1\,\Omega\) bridge arms and a central branch containing the \(1\,\text{F}\) capacitor(ignoring \(Z_1\)). For a balanced Wheatstone bridge: \[\frac{R_1}{R_2} = \frac{R_3}{R_4} \implies \frac{1\,\Omega}{1\,\Omega} = \frac{1\,\Omega}{1\,\Omega}\] Because the bridge is perfectly balanced, the potential difference across the central branch is zero. Consequently, no current flows through the central \(1\,\text{F}\) capacitor: \[\boxed{0}\]

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: A half-wave rectified sinusoidal waveform has a peak voltage of \(10\,\text{V}\). Its average value and the peak value of the fundamental component are respectively given by
questions.explanation:
A half-wave rectified sinusoidal waveform, \(v(t)\) is shown in \(Fig.Q3.87.1\) From the figure, we have \(v(t) = V_m \cos(\omega_0 t)\) for \(|t| \le (T_0/4)\) and \(V_m = 10\,\text{V}\). Period \(= T_0\) \(f_0 = 1/T_0 = \text{fundamental frequency} = 1^{\text{st}}\text{ harmonic}\) \(\omega_0 = 2\pi f_0\), \(n\omega_0 = n^{\text{th}}\text{ harmonic}\) Fourier series of \(v(t)\) is given by \[v(t) = a_0 + a_1 \cos(1\omega_0 t) + a_2 \cos(2\omega_0 t) + \dots\] \(a_0 = \text{Average (or mean or dc) value}\) \[a_0 = \frac{1}{T_0} \int_{T_0} v(t) \, dt\] \[= \frac{1}{T_0} \int_{-T_0/4}^{T_0/4} V_m \cos(\omega_0 t) \, dt = \frac{V_m}{\pi}\] Peak value of the fundamental component \[a_1 = \frac{2}{T_0} \int_{\langle T_0 \rangle} v(t)\cos(1\omega_0 t) \, dt\] \[= \frac{2}{T_0} \int_{-T_0/4}^{T_0/4} V_m \cos^2(\omega_0 t) \, dt = \frac{V_m}{2}\] Remember the answers: \[a_0 = \frac{V_m}{\pi}, \quad a_1 = \frac{V_m}{2}\] Substituting \(V_m = 10\,\text{V}\): \[\therefore a_0 = \frac{10}{\pi}\,\text{V}, \quad a_1 = 5\,\text{V}\] \[\boxed{\text{C) $\frac{10}{\pi}\,\text{V}, 5\,\text{V}$}}\]
Key points
  • The DC (average) component of a half-wave rectified sinusoidal signal with peak amplitude \(V_m\) is always \(V_m/\pi\).
  • The peak amplitude of the fundamental frequency component for a half-wave rectified sinusoid is always \(V_m/2\).

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: Laplace transform of the functions \(t u(t)\) and \(u(t) \sin(t)\) are respectively:
questions.explanation:
The given functions are standard signals frequently encountered in control systems and signal processing. 1. Laplace transform of \(t u(t)\):
The function \(t u(t)\) is known as the unit ramp signal. The general formula for the Laplace transform of \(t^n u(t)\) is \(\frac{n!}{s^{n+1}}\). Substituting \(n = 1\): \[\mathcal{L}\{t u(t)\} = \frac{1!}{s^{1+1}} = \frac{1}{s^2}\] 2. Laplace transform of \(u(t) \sin(t)\):
The function \(u(t) \sin(t)\) is a causal sinusoidal signal. The standard Laplace transform formula for a sine wave \(\sin(\omega t) u(t)\) is \(\frac{\omega}{s^2 + \omega^2}\). Here, the angular frequency is \(\omega = 1\): \[\mathcal{L}\{u(t) \sin(t)\} = \frac{1}{s^2 + 1^2} = \frac{1}{s^2 + 1}\] Therefore, the respective Laplace transforms are \(\frac{1}{s^2}\) and \(\frac{1}{s^2+1}\). \[\boxed{\text{C) }\frac{1}{s^2} , \frac{1}{s^2+1}}\]
Key points
  • Unit Ramp Signal: \(\mathcal{L}\{t u(t)\} = \frac{1}{s^2}\).
  • Causal Sine Function: \(\mathcal{L}\{\sin(\omega t) u(t)\} = \frac{\omega}{s^2 + \omega^2}\).
  • Causal Cosine Function: \(\mathcal{L}\{\cos(\omega t) u(t)\} = \frac{s}{s^2 + \omega^2}\).

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: Consider two energy levels: \(E_1\), \(E\,\text{ev}\) above the Fermi level and \(E_2\), \(E\,\text{ev}\) below the Fermi level. \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) are respectively the probability of \(E_1\) being occupied by an electron and \(E_2\) being empty. Then,
options: \(P_1\) & \(P_2\) depend on number of free electrons
questions.explanation: The probability \(P_1\) of an electron occupying \(E_1\) and \(P_2\) of \(E_2\) being empty are equal (\(P_1 = P_2\)) due to the symmetry of the Fermi-Dirac distribution around the Fermi level. Mathematically, \(f(E_F + \Delta E) = 1 - f(E_F - \Delta E)\), meaning the probability of finding an electron at a level above \(E_F\) equals the probability of finding a hole at the same distance below it. \[\boxed{(B) \, P_1 = P_2}\]

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: In an intrinsic semiconductor the free electron concentration depends on
options: width of the forbidden energy band of the semiconductor
questions.explanation:
According to the mass action law, the product of the free electron concentration (\(n\)) and the free hole concentration (\(p\)) is constant for a given semiconductor at a fixed temperature: \[n p = n_{i}^2\] The intrinsic carrier concentration (\(n_{i}\)) is strongly dependent on temperature (\(T\)). The relationship is given by: \[n_{i}^2 \propto T^3 e^{-E_{g}/kT} \implies n_{i} \propto T^{3/2}\] For an intrinsic semiconductor, since \(n = p = n_{i}\), the carrier concentration \(n\) follows the same temperature dependence: \[n \propto T^{3/2}\] \[\boxed{(C) \text{ temperature of the semiconductor}}\]
Key points
  • Intrinsic carrier concentration increases exponentially with temperature.

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: According to the Einstein relation, for any semiconductor the ratio of diffusion constant to mobility of carriers
options: depends upon the temperature of the semiconductor.
depends upon the type of the semiconductor.
varies with life time of the semiconductor.
questions.explanation:
The Einstein relation provides a fundamental link between the diffusion constant (\(D\)) and the mobility (\(\mu\)) of charge carriers in a semiconductor. The ratio is proportional to the absolute temperature: \[\frac{D_{n}}{\mu_{n}} = \frac{D_{p}}{\mu_{p}} = V_{T}\] The thermal voltage (\(V_{T}\)) is defined as: \[V_{T} = \frac{{k}T}{q} \approx \frac{T\text{ (in Kelvin)}}{11600}\] At room temperature (\(T = 300\,\text{K}\)), \(V_{T} \approx 25.86\,\text{mV}\). \[\boxed{(A) \text{ depends upon the temperature of the semiconductor.}}\]
Key points
  • This relation implies that carriers with higher mobility will also diffuse more rapidly.

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: Direct band gap semiconductors
options: exhibit short carrier life time and they are used for fabricating BJT's.
exhibit long carrier life time and they are used for fabricating BJT's.
exhibit short carrier life time and they are used for fabricating lasers.
exhibit long carrier life time and they are used for fabricating lasers.
questions.explanation:
Semiconductors are classified into Direct Band Gap (DBG) and Indirect Band Gap (IBG) materials based on the alignment of the conduction band minimum and valence band maximum in momentum space.
  • Direct Band Gap (e.g., GaAs): The maximum of the valence band and the minimum of the conduction band occur at the same value of the crystal momentum (\(k\)-vector). During recombination, an electron can transition directly, releasing energy primarily in the form of light (photons).
  • Indirect Band Gap (e.g., Si, Ge): The extrema occur at different \(k\)-values. Recombination requires a change in momentum (involving phonons), and energy is primarily released as heat.
Because DBG semiconductors exhibit high radiative recombination efficiency and short carrier lifetimes, they are used for fabricating Lasers and LEDs. \[\boxed{(C) \text{ exhibit short carrier life time and they are used for fabricating lasers.}}\]

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: The diffusion capacitance of a \(p\text{-}n\) junction
options: decreases with increasing current and increasing temperature.
decreases with decreasing current and increasing temperature.
increases with increasing current and increasing temperature.
does not depend on current and temperature.
questions.explanation:
The diffusion capacitance (\(C_D\)) decreases with decreasing forward current and increasing temperature. The formula for diffusion capacitance is given by: \[C_D = \frac{\tau}{r}\] where the dynamic internal forward resistance (\(r\)) of the diode is defined as: \[r = \frac{\eta V_T}{I_f}\] Substituting the expression for \(r\) into the capacitance formula yields: \[C_D = \frac{\tau I_f}{\eta V_T}\] Since the thermal voltage is defined as \(V_T = \frac{kT}{q}\), where \(k\) is the Boltzmann constant and \(T\) is the absolute temperature: \[C_D = \frac{\tau I_f q}{\eta k T}\] From this relation, it is clear that: \[C_D \propto I_f\] \[C_D \propto \frac{1}{T}\] Therefore, the diffusion capacitance is directly proportional to the forward current (\(I_f\)) and inversely proportional to the absolute temperature (\(T\)). \[\boxed{(B) \text{ decreases with decreasing current and increasing temperature}}\]
Key points
  • Diffusion capacitance (\(C_D\)) is dominant under forward-biased conditions due to minority carrier storage.
  • The parameter \(\tau\) represents the mean carrier lifetime of the minority charge carriers.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse the temperature dependence of diffusion capacitance (\(C_D \propto T^{-1}\)) with depletion capacitance, which has a different mathematical relationship governed by the built-in potential.

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: In figure if the CMRR of the operational amplifier is \(60\text{ dB}\), then the magnitude of the output voltage is _______ \(\text{mV}\).
questions.explanation:
Given \(\text{CMRR}\) of given Op-Amp is \(60\,\text{dB}\). Op-Amp circuit without bridge is shown below, From above circuit, differential gain is given by, \[|A_d| = \frac{R_2}{R_1} = 100\] Bridge circuit of given Op-Amp circuit is shown below, In the above circuit bridge is balance. Hence, \[V_A = \frac{R}{R+R} \times 2 = 1\,\text{Volt}\] \[V_B = \frac{R}{R+R} \times 2 = 1\,\text{Volt}\] Differential input voltage is given by, \[V_d = V_A - V_B = 0\] Output voltage when \(\text{CMRR} \neq \infty\), is given by, \[V_0 = A_d V_d + A_c V_c\] Since, \(V_d = 0\). Hence, \(V_0 = A_c V_c \quad \dots \text{(i)}\) Common mode input voltage is given by, \[V_c = \frac{V_A + V_B}{2} = 1\,\text{Volt}\] Since, \(\text{CMRR}|_{dB} = 20\log(\text{CMRR})\) \[60 = 20\log \text{CMRR}\] \[\text{CMRR} = (10)^{60/20} = 1000\] \[\text{CMRR} = \left| \frac{A_d}{A_c} \right|\] Hence, \(A_c = \frac{A_d}{\text{CMRR}} = \frac{100}{1000} = 0.1\) From equation (i), \[V_0 = 0.1 \times 1 = 0.1\,\text{Volt} = 100\,\text{mV}\] \[\boxed{V_0 = 100\text{ mV}}\]
Key points
  • Common Mode Rejection Ratio (CMRR): It is defined as the ratio of differential mode gain (\(A_d\)) to common mode gain (\(A_c\)). Expressed in decibels, \(\text{CMRR (dB)} = 20 \log_{10}(|A_d/A_c|)\).
  • Non-Ideal Output Voltage: For an op-amp with a finite CMRR, the output voltage is a superposition of both differential and common-mode amplifications: \(V_0 = A_d V_d + A_c V_c\), where \(V_d = V_+ - V_-\) is the differential input and \(V_c = (V_+ + V_-)/2\) is the common-mode input.
  • Balanced Bridge: A balanced Wheatstone bridge (\(R_1/R_2 = R_3/R_4\)) produces zero differential voltage (\(V_A = V_B = V_d = 0\)), meaning the entire input to the subsequent differential amplifier acts as a pure common-mode signal.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.ref: Logic Gates and Boolean Algebra Q1
questions.question: For the circuit shown below the output \(F\) is given by
questions.explanation: All three gates are EX-OR gates, and the input \(X\) is applied to one input of each gate. Let the outputs of the three EX-OR gates be \(Y_{1}\), \(Y_{2}\), and \(F\). \[Y_{1}=X\oplus X=0\] The second gate gives \[Y_{2}=Y_{1}\oplus X=0\oplus X=X\] The final gate gives \[F=Y_{2}\oplus X=X\oplus X=0\] \[\boxed{\text{(b) }F=0}\]

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: The subtraction of a binary number \(Y\) from another binary number \(X\), done by adding the 2's complement of \(Y\) to \(X\), results in a binary number without overflow. This implies that the result is:
options: negative and is in normal form
negative and is in 2's complement form
positive and is in normal form
positive and is in 2's complement form
questions.explanation:
Binary subtraction is performed as \[X-Y=X+\left(\text{2's complement of }Y\right)\] If the addition is completed without overflow, the result can be interpreted as follows:
  • If there is an end carry, it is discarded and the result is positive in its normal binary form. \(\checkmark\)
  • If there is no end carry, the result is negative and remains in 2's complement form. \(\checkmark\)
Hence, \[\boxed{\text{(b) and (c)}}\]
Key points
  • Binary subtraction is performed by adding the 2's complement of the subtrahend.
  • End carry present \(\Rightarrow\) positive result in normal binary form.
  • No end carry \(\Rightarrow\) negative result in 2's complement form.
  • The question states that no overflow occurs.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse end carry with overflow; they are different concepts.
  • Do not convert a negative result from 2's complement unless its magnitude is specifically asked.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question:
Statement for Linked Answer Questions Q5.87.1 and Q5.87.2 (Total 8 Marks): A 2-input up/down synchronous counter using two toggle flip-flops is shown in plain figure. The counter's sequence is to be controlled by the input \(M\) as follows: For \(M=1\), sequence of \(Q_1, Q_0\) is ..00, 01, 10, 11, 00, 01....... For \(M=0\), sequence of \(Q_1, Q_0\) is ..00, 11, 10, 01, 00, 11.......

Design the necessary feedback logic for \(T_1\) and \(T_0\).
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
To design the feedback logic for the synchronous up/down counter, we determine the toggle inputs \(T_1\) and \(T_0\) using a state transition table.
  1. State Transition and Excitation Table:
    The desired counting sequence behaves as an up-counter when \(M = 1\) (\(00 \rightarrow 01 \rightarrow 10 \rightarrow 11\)) and a down-counter when \(M = 0\) (\(00 \rightarrow 11 \rightarrow 10 \rightarrow 01\)). Using the characteristic behavior of a \(T\) flip-flop (\(T = 1\) toggles state, \(T = 0\) maintains state), we create the excitation table:
    \(M\)\(Q_1\)\(Q_0\)\(Q_{1(\text{next})}\)\(Q_{0(\text{next})}\)\(T_1\)\(T_0\)
    0001111
    0010001
    0100111
    0111001
    1000101
    1011011
    1101101
    1110011
  2. Logic Expression Derivation:
    • For \(T_0\): The column is 1 for all combinations. Therefore, \(T_0 = 1\).
    • For \(T_1\): Let us simplify using a kmap: \[T_1 = \overline{M}\,\overline{Q}_0 + MQ_0 = M \odot Q_0\]
\[\boxed{T_1 = M \odot Q_0, \ T_0 = 1}\]
Key points
  • Synchronous Toggle Condition: The LSB (\(Q_0\)) always toggles on every clock edge, so \(T_0 = 1\).
  • Directional Control: The next stage toggles based on the combination of the mode control \(M\) and the current state of \(Q_0\).

questions.question:
Statement for Linked Answer Questions Q5.87.1 and Q5.87.2 (Total 8 Marks): A 2-input up/down synchronous counter using two toggle flip-flops is shown in plain figure. The counter's sequence is to be controlled by the input \(M\) as follows: For \(M=1\), sequence of \(Q_1, Q_0\) is ..00, 01, 10, 11, 00, 01....... For \(M=0\), sequence of \(Q_1, Q_0\) is ..00, 11, 10, 01, 00, 11.......

Realize the feedback logic using inverters and 4-input multiplexers only. Use \(Q_1\) and \(Q_0\) as the control inputs of the multiplexer with \(Q_1\) as the MSB.
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
To realize the expressions \(T_1 = \overline{M}\,\overline{Q}_0 + MQ_0\) and \(T_0 = 1\) using 4-to-1 multiplexers with \(Q_1Q_0\) as selection lines (\(Q_1\) as MSB, \(Q_0\) as LSB):
  1. Multiplexer Implementation for \(T_1\):
    We map the function \(T_1(Q_1, Q_0)\) by evaluating its required input data lines (\(I_0, I_1, I_2, I_3\)) corresponding to the selection inputs \(Q_1Q_0\):
  2. Multiplexer Implementation for \(T_0\):
    Since \(T_0 = 1\) unconditionally, all four data inputs of its multiplexer are tied directly to logic high level:
\[\boxed{\text{Inputs for } T_1: \{\overline{M}, M, \overline{M}, M\}; \ \text{Inputs for } T_0: \{1, 1, 1, 1\}}\]
Key points
  • 4-to-1 MUX Logic: Implementing a function via MUX mapping avoids routing overhead by directly assigning the remaining single literal (\(M\) or \(\overline{M}\)) to the data terminal inputs.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: Choose the correct statements relating to the circuit of plain figure
options: For \(V_i = 0\text{V}\), P can be either 0 or 1.
questions.explanation:
The circuit consists of two voltage comparators driving a cross-coupled NOR latch. Let the output of the top comparator be \(S\) and the output of the bottom comparator be \(R\).
  • Top Comparator: The non-inverting terminal (\(+\)) is connected to \(V_i\) and the inverting terminal (\(-\)) is connected to \(+2\,\text{V}\). \[S = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } V_i > +2\,\text{V} \\ 0 & \text{if } V_i < +2\,\text{V} \end{cases}\]
  • Bottom Comparator: The inverting terminal (\(-\)) is connected to \(V_i\) and the non-inverting terminal (\(+\)) is connected to \(-1\,\text{V}\). \[R = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } V_i < -1\,\text{V} \\ 0 & \text{if } V_i > -1\,\text{V} \end{cases}\]
Let us evaluate all the four options:
  1. Checking Option A: For \(V_i = +3\,\text{V}\), we have \(V_i > +2\,\text{V} \implies S = 1\) and \(V_i > -1\,\text{V} \implies R = 0\). For a NOR latch, when \(S = 1\) and \(R = 0\), the latch resets, forcing \(P = 0\) and \(Q = 1\). Thus, statement (A) is incorrect.
  2. Checking Option B: Following the same conditions as Option A (\(V_i = +3\,\text{V} \implies S = 1, R = 0\)), the latch resets giving \(P = 0\). Thus, statement (B) is correct.
  3. Checking Option C: For \(V_i = -2\,\text{V}\), we have \(V_i < +2\,\text{V} \implies S = 0\) and \(V_i < -1\,\text{V} \implies R = 1\). When \(S = 0\) and \(R = 1\), the NOR latch enters the set state, forcing \(P = 1\) and \(Q = 0\). Therefore, \(P\) cannot be \(0\), making statement (C) incorrect.
  4. Checking Option D: For \(V_i = 0\,\text{V}\), we have \(V_i < +2\,\text{V} \implies S = 0\) and \(V_i > -1\,\text{V} \implies R = 0\). When both inputs to the NOR latch are \(0\), the circuit enters the Hold State (\(P_{next} = P\)). Thus, \(P\) depends entirely on its previous state and can be either \(0\) or \(1\). Hence, statement (D) is correct.
(B) For \(V_i = +3\,\text{V}, P = 0\)
(D) For \(V_i = 0\,\text{V}\), P can be either 0 or 1.
Key points
  • NOR Latch Truth Table:
    • \(S=0, R=0 \implies\) Hold state (output maintains its previous state of \(0\) or \(1\)).
    • \(S=1, R=0 \implies\) Reset output \(P = 0\).
    • \(S=0, R=1 \implies\) Set output \(P = 1\).

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: A ripple counter using negative edge-triggered D-flip flops is shown in plain figure. The flip-flops are cleared to '0' by a '0' at the R input. The feedback logic is to be designed to obtain the count sequence shown in the same figure. The correct feedback logic is:
questions.explanation:
The problem requires designing feedback logic to truncate a 3-bit ripple counter so that it follows a Modulo-6 counting sequence: \[000 \rightarrow 001 \rightarrow 010 \rightarrow 011 \rightarrow 100 \rightarrow 101 \rightarrow (000)\]
  1. Identification of the Reset State:
    The counter cycles through 6 valid states (\(0\) to \(5\) in decimal). The next sequential state that would normally occur is \(6_{10} = 110_2\). Therefore, when the states reach \(Q_2Q_1Q_0 = 110\), the counter must immediately clear all flip-flops back to \(000\).
  2. Active-Low Reset Analysis:
    The problem statement specifies that the flip-flops are cleared to '0' by applying a logic low level ('0') at the active-low reset inputs (\(R\)). Thus, the output of the feedback logic \(F\) must satisfy:
    • \(F = 0\) when \(Q_2 = 1, Q_1 = 1, Q_0 = 0\) (the state \(110_2\)).
    • \(F = 1\) for all other valid counting states (\(000\) through \(101\)) to allow normal operation.
  3. Formulating the Logic Function:
    To generate a \(0\) uniquely for the minterm corresponding to \(Q_2Q_1\overline{Q}_0\), a standard NAND implementation is used: \[F = \overline{Q_2 \cdot Q_1 \cdot \overline{Q}_0}\]
This matches the expression given in option (A). \[\boxed{\text{(A) } F = \overline{Q_2 Q_1 \overline{Q}_0}}\]
Key points
  • Asynchronous Truncation: An asynchronous clear mechanism causes a temporary glitch state (here, \(110\)) that is quickly wiped out as soon as the reset logic propagates back to the flip-flop clear terminals.
  • Active-Low Conventions: NAND gates are naturally well-suited as decode logic for active-low clear systems since they output a \(0\) only when the target transient combination is matched.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question:
Statement for Linked Answer Questions Q6.87.1, Q6.87.2, Q6.87.3 and Q6.87.4 (Total 8 Marks): The circuit diagram of a \(2\text{ bit}\) A to D converter is shown in figure below. The combinational logic is to be designed to provide a natural binary representation using \(D_1\) and \(D_0\) for the analog input \(V_i\). \(D_1\) is to be the most significant bit.

Draw the Karnaugh maps for \(D_1\) and \(D_0\) in terms of \(C_2\), \(C_1\) and \(C_0\)
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
The voltage reference levels at the non-inverting inputs of the comparators are: \[V_0 = \frac{V_{\text{CC}}}{4}, \quad V_1 = \frac{2V_{\text{CC}}}{4}, \quad V_2 = \frac{3V_{\text{CC}}}{4}\] The truth table relating the analog input \(V_i\), the comparator outputs, and the natural binary outputs \(D_1 D_0\) is:
Analog Input \(V_i\)\(C_2\)\(C_1\)\(C_0\)\(D_1\)\(D_0\)
\(0 < V_i < \frac{V_{\text{CC}}}{4}\)00000
\(\frac{V_{\text{CC}}}{4} < V_i < \frac{2V_{\text{CC}}}{4}\)00101
\(\frac{2V_{\text{CC}}}{4} < V_i < \frac{3V_{\text{CC}}}{4}\)01110
\(V_i > \frac{3V_{\text{CC}}}{4}\)11111
The rest of the terms are Don't care terms(X) The Karnaugh maps for \(D_1\) and \(D_0\) in terms of \(C_2, C_1, C_0\) are shown below:
  • For \(D_1\): \[D_1 = C_1\]
  • For \(D_0\): \[D_0 = C_0\,\overline{C_1} + C_2\]
Key points

questions.ref: Logic Families and Semiconductor Memories Q1
questions.question: Given that for a logic family, \(V_{OH}\) is the minimum output high-level voltage \(V_{OL}\) is the maximum output low-level voltage \(V_{IH}\) is the minimum acceptable input high-level voltage and \(V_{IL}\) is the maximum acceptable input low-level voltage. The correct relationship is:
questions.explanation:
To determine the correct relationship between the input and output voltage levels of a valid digital logic family, we analyze the definition of the critical voltage parameters necessary to ensure reliable data transmission and positive noise margins. A properly functioning logic family must satisfy conditions that allow a driving gate's output to be cleanly interpreted by a receiving gate's input, even in the presence of signal degradation or noise. The voltage specifications are defined as follows:
  • \(V_{OH}\): The minimum guaranteed output high-level voltage from a driving gate.
  • \(V_{IH}\): The minimum accepted input high-level voltage recognized by a receiving gate as logic 1.
  • \(V_{IL}\): The maximum accepted input low-level voltage recognized by a receiving gate as logic 0.
  • \(V_{OL}\): The maximum guaranteed output low-level voltage from a driving gate.
For a stable digital system with non-zero (positive) noise margins:
  1. High-Level Noise Immunity: The output high voltage must exceed the required input high voltage to accommodate noise drops: \[V_{OH} > V_{IH} \implies (NM)_H = V_{OH} - V_{IH} > 0\]
  2. Low-Level Noise Immunity: The input low voltage threshold must be higher than the maximum output low voltage to ensure safety against noise spikes: \[V_{IL} > V_{OL} \implies (NM)_L = V_{IL} - V_{OL} > 0\]
Combining these relations with the absolute voltage separation between logic high and logic low levels (\(V_{IH} > V_{IL}\)), we establish the complete hierarchical sequence: \[V_{OH} > V_{IH} > V_{IL} > V_{OL}\] \[\boxed{\text{(B) } V_{OH} > V_{IH} > V_{IL} > V_{OL}}\]
Key points
ParameterOperational Requirement
High-Level Noise Margin\((NM)_H = V_{OH} - V_{IH} \quad (\text{Must be } > 0)\)
Low-Level Noise Margin\((NM)_L = V_{IL} - V_{OL} \quad (\text{Must be } > 0)\)
  • Invalid Regions: The region between \(V_{IH}\) and \(V_{IL}\) represents an undefined or transition region where the logic state cannot be reliably determined.
  • Noise Immunity Implications: If a logic family violates this hierarchical ordering (e.g., \(V_{OH} < V_{IH}\)), it results in a negative noise margin, causing systemic data corruption during standard operations.

Among the TTL Families, family requires considerably less power than the standard TTL (74XX) and also has comparable propagation delay.
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
To fill in the blanks for the given common data statements concerning various digital logic families, we evaluate their power-delay product metrics and supply voltage requirements. Among the different configurations within the Transistor-Transistor Logic (TTL) sub-families:
  • Standard TTL (74XX) features a balanced speed but suffers from relatively high power dissipation.
  • Low-power TTL (74LXX) drastically decreases power usage, but at the expense of significantly increasing the propagation delay (making it much slower).
  • Low-power Schottky TTL (74LSXX) incorporates Schottky diode clamping across base-collector junctions to prevent transistor saturation. This design element yields a sub-family that requires considerably lower power dissipation (\(\approx 2\,\text{mW}\) per gate compared to \(10\,\text{mW}\) for standard TTL) while preserving a comparable propagation delay (\(\approx 9\,\text{ns}\)).
Therefore, the missing term is 74LS

questions.question:
Statement for Linked Answer Questions Q7.87.2 & Q7.87.3: Fill in the blanks of the statements below concerning the following Logic Families: Standard TTL(74XX), Low power TTL(74LXX) Low power schottky TTL(74LSXX), Schottky TTL(74SXXX), Emitter coupled Logic (ECL), CMOS

Only the family can operate over a wide range of power supply voltages.
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
Considering the operational requirements for supply voltages across the listed logic structures:
  • Bipolar-based families like TTL and ECL demand tightly controlled supply levels. For instance, standard TTL gates operate reliably only within a narrow toleration window of \(5\,\text{V} \pm 5\%\) (\(4.75\,\text{V}\) to \(5.25\,\text{V}\)).
  • Conversely, Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor (CMOS) configurations function independently of a highly precise supply voltage because their complementary switching behavior relies primarily on voltage ratios rather than fixed forward-bias diode voltages. Standard CMOS integrated circuits can seamlessly operate over a broad range of supply levels, typically spanning from \(3\,\text{V}\) to \(15\,\text{V}\).
Therefore, the missing term is CMOS.

Common Data for Questions Q2.11.1 and Q6.11.1: The input-output transfer function of a plant \(H(s) = \dfrac{100}{s(s+10)^{2}}\). The plant is placed in a unity negative feedback configuration as shown in the figure below. The 2nd Question is given in Unit VI (Q6.11.1)

For the system shown in figure the transfer function \(C(s)/R(s)\) is equal to
questions.explanation:
Method 1
Using Mason's Gain Formula: \[\frac{C(s)}{R(s)} = \frac{\dfrac{10}{s(s+1)}}{1 - \left( -\dfrac{10}{s(s+1)} - \dfrac{10s}{s(s+1)} \right)} = \frac{10}{s(s+1) + 10 + 10s} = \frac{10}{s^2 + 11s + 10}\]
Method 2
Using Block Diagram Reduction: The inner loop with feedback gain \(s\) has a transfer function \(G_{inner}(s)\): \[G_{inner}(s) = \frac{\dfrac{10}{s(s+1)}}{1 + \dfrac{10}{s(s+1)} \times s} = \frac{10}{s(s+1) + 10s}\] \[\frac{C(s)}{R(s)} = \frac{G_{inner}(s)}{1 + G_{inner}(s) \times 1} = \frac{\dfrac{10}{s^2 + 11s}}{1 + \dfrac{10}{s^2 + 11s}} = \frac{10}{s^2 + 11s + 10}\]
\[\boxed{(B) \ \ \frac{10}{s^2 + 11s + 10}}\]

questions.question: The unity feedback system shown in fig. has:
questions.explanation:
For Unit Step Input:
The steady-state error (\(e_{ss}\)) is given by: \[e_{ss} = \frac{A}{1 + K_p}\] Where \(K_p\) is the position error constant: \[K_p = \lim_{s \to 0} G(s)H(s)\] Given the system forward path transfer function implicitly contains a pole at the origin, i.e., \(G(s)H(s) = \dfrac{K}{s(s+10)}\): \[K_p = \lim_{s \to 0} \frac{K}{s(s+10)} = \infty\] \[e_{ss} = \frac{1}{1 + \infty} = 0\] Hence, the system has zero steady-state error for a step input. For Unit Ramp Input:
The steady-state error (\(e_{ss}\)) is given by: \[e_{ss} = \frac{A}{K_v}\] Where \(K_v\) is the velocity error constant: \[K_v = \lim_{s \to 0} s \cdot G(s)H(s)\] \[K_v = \lim_{s \to 0} s \cdot \frac{K}{s(s+10)} = \frac{K}{10}\] Substituting \(K_v\) back into the error equation for a unit ramp input (\(A = 1\)): \[e_{ss} = \frac{1}{K/10} = \frac{10}{K}\] Thus, the steady-state error for a ramp input is \(\dfrac{10}{K}\). \[\boxed{\text{(A) \ Zero steady state position error}}\]

Also, variance is unaffected by sign inversion. \[\mathrm{Var}(aX)=a^2\sigma_x^2\]Hence, \[\mathrm{Var}(-kX)=k^2\sigma_x^2\] \[\mathrm{Var}(-kX) = E\left[(-kX)^2\right] - \left[E(-kX)\right]^2\] \[= k^2E(X^2) - \left[-kE(X)\right]^2\] \[= k^2E(X^2) - k^2[E(X)]^2\] \[= k^2\left(E(X^2)-[E(X)]^2\right)\] \[= k^2\sigma_x^2\] \[\boxed{(D) \mathrm{Var}(-kX)=k^2\sigma_x^2 }\]

questions.question: An electrostatic field is said to be conservative when:
options: The divergence of the field is equal to zero.
The curl of the field is equal to zero.
The curl of the field is equal to \(-\dfrac{\partial E}{\partial t^2}\).
The Laplacian of the field is equal to \(\mu\varepsilon \dfrac{\partial^2 E}{\partial t^2}\).
questions.explanation:
An electrostatic field \(\vec{E}\) is defined as a conservative field because the work done in moving a charge along a closed path is zero. This property is mathematically expressed by the closed line integral: \[\oint_C \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{l} = 0\] By applying Stokes' theorem, which relates the line integral of a vector field over a closed curve \(C\) to the surface integral of its curl over the surface \(S\) bounded by \(C\): \[\oint_C \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{l} = \iint_S (
abla 	imes \vec{E}) \cdot d\vec{s}\] Equating these two expressions, we obtain: \[\iint_S (
abla 	imes \vec{E}) \cdot d\vec{s} = 0\] Since this must hold for any arbitrary surface \(S\), the curl of the electrostatic field must be zero: \[ oxed{(B) : 
abla 	imes \vec{E} = 0}\]

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: For an electromagnetic wave incident from one medium to a second medium, total reflection takes place when
options: the angle of incidence is equal to the Brewster angle with \(E\) field perpendicular to the plane of incidence.
the angle of incidence is equal to the Brewster angle with \(E\) field parallel to the plane of incidence.
the angle of incidence is equal to the critical angle with the wave moving from the denser medium to a rarer medium.
the angle of incidence is equal to the critical angle with the wave moving from a rarer medium to a rarer medium.
questions.explanation:
The critical angle \(\theta_{c}\) for an interface between two dielectric media is defined as the angle of incidence for which the angle of refraction is \(90^{\circ}\). It is expressed in terms of refractive indices \(n_{1}, n_{2}\) or relative permittivities \(\epsilon_{r1}, \epsilon_{r2}\) as: \[\theta_{c} = \sin^{-1} \left( \frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} \right) = \sin^{-1} \sqrt{\frac{\epsilon_{r2}}{\epsilon_{r1}}}\] For total internal reflection to occur, two conditions must be satisfied:
  1. The wave must propagate from a denser medium to a rarer medium, implying \(\epsilon_{r1} > \epsilon_{r2}\) (or \(n_{1} > n_{2}\)).
  2. The angle of incidence \(\theta_{i}\) must be greater than or equal to the critical angle \(\theta_{c}\):
\[\theta_{i} \geq \theta_{c}\] Substituting the expression for \(\theta_{c}\), we obtain the final condition for total internal reflection: \[\boxed{(C):\theta_{i} \geq \sin^{-1} \sqrt{\frac{\epsilon_{r2}}{\epsilon_{r1}}}}\]

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: A transmission line of real characteristic impedance is terminated with an unknown load. The measured value of VSWR on the line is equal to \(2\) and a voltage minimum point is found to be at the load. The load impedance is then
questions.explanation:
For a lossless transmission line terminated with a load impedance \(Z_{L}\), the location of voltage extrema (maxima and minima) depends on the nature of the load. If voltage maxima (\(V_{max}\)) or voltage minima (\(V_{min}\)) occur exactly at the load, it implies that the load impedance \(Z_{L}\) is purely resistive. The relationship between the load resistance \(Z_{L}\) and the characteristic impedance of the line \(Z_{0}\) is as follows:
  • If \(Z_{L} > Z_{0}\): The load is an open-circuit-like termination, and a voltage maximum (\(V_{max}\)) occurs at the load.
  • If \(Z_{L} < Z_{0}\): The load is a short-circuit-like termination, and a voltage minimum (\(V_{min}\)) occurs at the load.
\[\boxed{(C):\text {purely resistive} }\]
Key points
  • For a purely resistive load \(Z_{L}\), the reflection coefficient \(\Gamma\) is real.
  • When \(Z_{L} > Z_{0}\), \(\Gamma > 0\), causing constructive interference at the load (Voltage Max).
  • When \(Z_{L} < Z_{0}\), \(\Gamma < 0\), causing destructive interference at the load (Voltage Min).
  • If \(Z_{L} = Z_{0}\), the line is matched, \(\Gamma = 0\), and no standing waves exist; the voltage is constant along the entire line.

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: The cut-off frequency of a waveguide depends upon
options: the dielectric property of the medium in the waveguide.
the characteristic impedance of the waveguide.
the transverse and axial components of the fields.
questions.explanation:
The cut-off frequency (\(f_{c}\)) for a mode (\(mn\)) in a rectangular waveguide filled with a dielectric medium is determined by the waveguide dimensions (\(a, b\)) and the properties of the medium (\(\mu, \epsilon\)): \[f_{c} = \frac{v_{o}}{2} \sqrt{\left(\frac{m}{a}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{n}{b}\right)^{2}}\] where the velocity of light in the medium is: \[v_{o} = \frac{c}{\sqrt{\mu_{r}\epsilon_{r}}}\] Substituting \(v_{o}\) into the cut-off frequency expression: \[f_{c} = \frac{c}{2\sqrt{\mu_{r}\epsilon_{r}}} \sqrt{\left(\frac{m}{a}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{n}{b}\right)^{2}}\] From this expression, it is evident that:
  • \(f_{c}\) is inversely proportional to the square root of the product of relative permeability (\(\mu_{r}\)) and permittivity (\(\epsilon_{r}\)).
  • Therefore, \(f_{c} \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_{r}\epsilon_{r}}}\).
\[\boxed{(A,B)}\]
